idiom_name: key-based per-thread collection behind a global accessor (TS Object Proxy over the TS Object Collection)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: allocate one key per thread-specific datum once per process, keep a per-thread collection that maps keys to that thread's objects, and expose a single access point whose getter returns - and lazily creates - the calling thread's object while hiding both the key and the collection from callers (POSA2's TS Object Proxy over the TS Object Collection). Key registration and per-thread construction must be idempotent across threads: create the key once, and let each thread build its own object on first access. Provide a cleanup hook that runs when a thread exits, and in pooled environments also when a work item finishes, because otherwise the value outlives the work that produced it. Prefer the language's own construct where one exists (thread_local, ThreadLocal, thread_local!, @ThreadLocal, threadDictionary, threading.local) and reserve the hand-built registry for environments that offer only raw OS keys.
code_sketch:
key = key_create(destroy=factory.dispose)   # once per process

def current():
    obj = get_specific(key)          # per-thread lookup, no lock
    if obj is None:                  # this thread has no instance yet
        obj = factory.create()
        set_specific(key, obj)
    return obj                       # logically global, physically per-thread
pitfalls: Key registration is not idempotent by default (POSIX creates a new key on every call), so guard it with a once-per-process initialiser.
The thread-exit hook is the only automatic cleanup; relying on it in a thread pool leaks values from one work item into the next.
Hand-rolling the collection as a map keyed by a thread identifier reintroduces locking on the hot path and breaks on runtimes that virtualise or reuse threads.

Performing I/O or calling arbitrary code inside a TLS destructor is unsafe: POSIX allows only async-signal-unsafe operations in destructors, and Rust aborts the process if a thread-local destructor panics.
Mixing C++ thread_local with POSIX TSD inside the same destructor chain is unsafe on glibc because glibc destroys C++ thread_local objects before thread-specific data.

In runtimes that multiplex many tasks onto one OS thread (event loops, goroutine or structured-concurrency schedulers, JVM virtual threads), the proxy's unit of identity is wrong: the same access point serves different logical tasks at different times, so one task's value is read - and overwritten - by another. Bind the storage to the task or scope instead, or pass the value explicitly.
